Euphorbia epithymoides.name_note: Euphorbia polychroma is the name this plant is still widely sold under. NC State says much of the literature treats E. polychroma as synonymous with E. epithymoides, but also says POWO reverses the direction (E. epithymoides subsp. epithymoides is the synonym of E. polychroma). RHS's dedicated Euphorbia epithymoides page lists the name status as Correct. The given name is kept as the accepted name because the RHS page for it says Correct.
Euphorbia epithymoides.toxicity_detail: NC State (Poison block, heading "Poisonous to Humans", so the rating is human-scoped): Poison Severity Low; the page also says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Poison Symptoms: "The milky white latex sap found in all plant parts can cause mild to severe contact dermatitis. If contact with the eyes occurs the sap can cause temporary to permanent damage to the cornea. If eaten, blistering can occur on lips and oral mucosa. Avoid ingesting plant parts and keep plants away from pets and children." Poison Toxic Principle: Diterpene esters in milky latex. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part (full list): Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Sap/Juice, Stems. Handling warning from the description: wear gloves and eye protection because the milky sap is toxic to skin and eyes. The description also says all parts are toxic if ingested and to monitor small children and pets. NC State's separate Problems tags (not the Poison block) are: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs. These Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags are the only cat/dog scoping, and they are what supports toxic_to_pets=true. The page's tag list also carries #poisonous, #poisonous if ingested and #contact dermatitis. Plant Type values (three): Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. NC State's Edibility field reads: Stems exude a slightly toxic, milky sap when cut. RHS (Potentially harmful Humans/Pets) is unscoped to cat or dog: IRRITANT to skin/eye; harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.

NC State's page title parenthetical leads with Brown-Eyed Susan, and its alphabetized Common Name(s) list also starts with Brown-Eyed Susan (Thin Leaved Coneflower, Three-lobed Coneflower follow). RHS's subtitle is brown-eyed Susan, with three-leaved coneflower under Other common names. MoBot's single Common Name line reads three-leaved coneflower, while its Noteworthy Characteristics prose says the plant is commonly called brown-eyed Susan and lists thin-leaved coneflower and three-lobed coneflower as other names. unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: none of the three pages read (NC State, MoBot, RHS) names any toxicity, poison part, or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag for Rudbeckia triloba; no value taken from the genus or from R. hirta, so both are null.
is_edible: no page read addresses eating this plant. NC State's food source tags (herbage, nectar, pollen, fall, hard mast fruit) are wildlife tags, so is_edible is null (no record).

Life cycle, stated exactly: NC State's Description calls it an herbaceous biennial or short-lived perennial, its Life Cycle field lists Biennial and Perennial, and its Plant Type field lists four values (Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant, Wildflower). outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field also lists Partial Shade (2-6 hours) and its prose says it will grow in light shade, but MoBot's structured Sun field and RHS's Position field list full sun only (MoBot treats light shade as a tolerance in prose). part_shade is therefore left out.
direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's hour range comes only from its site-wide light legend, not species prose, so it is not used.
soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: RHS gives pH as Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, which is categorical, and no page gives numeric bounds, so both are null.

water_regime and other watering fields: MoBot's structured Water field reads Medium, which is mid-scale and does not support keep_moist. No page frames watering as a dry-down pattern, and this is an in-ground perennial, so water_regime, water_dry_down_target, check depth and day-interval fields are null.

Size disagreement: NC State Dimensions give Height 3-5 ft and Width 1-1.5 ft (used). MoBot says Height 2.00 to 3.00 feet (prose: typically 2-3 ft, less frequently to 5 ft) and Spread 1.00 to 1.50 feet. RHS says Max Height 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in) and Max Spread 0.5-1 metres.

chill_damage_f, day/night temperatures, humidity, light foot-candles, fertilizing: not addressed by any page read. NC State lists USDA zones 4a-8b and MoBot zones 4 to 8, which are hardiness ratings, not damage onset temperatures.

Meadow Phlox was chosen as the name both dedicated pages use. NC State's 'is often confused with' module for this page lists Phlox carolina.
unknowns: Mildew (requested NC State note): NC State says this phlox has better mildew resistance than P. paniculata but still needs good air circulation, and overhead watering should be avoided; root rot and spider mites can be an issue. MoBot likewise calls it a good alternative to the more mildew-susceptible garden phlox (P. paniculata) but says plants need good air circulation to combat potential powdery mildew.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: neither the NC State page nor the MoBot page for Phlox maculata carries a Poison block or any Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag or toxicity statement. is_edible left null: neither page addresses eating the plant (NC State's ethnobotany note is a root infusion used as a wash, not food).

Veronicastrum virginicum.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's page-title parenthetical reads (Bowman’s Root, Culver's Root), an alphabetized list, while its Description opens with Culver's Root; MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose says 'commonly called Culver's root'; RHS's dedicated page subtitle is Culver's root and its Other common names field lists Bowman's root among others. Culver's Root is used. RHS lists Veronica virginica as a synonym of this species.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: none of the three admissible dedicated pages (NC State, MoBot, RHS) carries a Poison block, a Problem for Cats/Dogs tag, or any statement that the plant is poisonous to cats, dogs or any animal. The only related text is medicinal-use history: NC State's Uses (Ethnobotany) says the Cherokee, Iroquois, Chippewa and Menominee used the plant as an analgesic, cathartic (accelerated defecation), emetic (induces vomiting), and for coughs, fevers, rheumatism and childbirth; MoBot says 'Root has been used medicinally as a cathartic.' These are historical medicinal uses, not a toxicity finding for pets or people, and no dose or plant-part toxicity scope is given beyond MoBot's 'Root'. The root's purgative history is a reason for caution but is not recorded as a toxicity claim.
is_edible left null: no admissible source says any part is grown or used for food; the cathartic/emetic uses are medicinal, not food.
is_houseplant left null: all sources treat it as an in-ground native herbaceous perennial for borders, meadows and rain gardens; none addresses indoor culture.

outdoor_sun_exposure lists only full_sun: NC State's structured Light field and MoBot's Sun field both say full sun. RHS also lists Partial shade (Position: Full sun, Partial shade) and MoBot's culture text says it 'Tolerates light shade' as a conditional aside; because the two North American structured fields give full sun only, part_sun/part_shade is left out and disclosed here.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figure is the generic NC State light-category legend wording, not species-specific prose.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State ticks Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), all open-ended or spanning, and RHS says pH Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no bound is supportable.

Sedum acre.name_note: Admissible sources split on the primary common name. NC State's description opens with "Moss stonecrop", while its alphabetized Common Name(s) list (shown as the page-title parenthetical) begins with Biting Stonecrop and also includes Moss Stonecrop; RHS's page title leads with "biting stonecrop"; MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose says "common stonecrop or gold moss stonecrop". Moss Stonecrop is used here as the app name, led by the NC State description; the bare name Stonecrop is not used.
Sedum acre.toxicity_detail: No admissible source names cats or dogs for this species, so toxic_to_pets is left null. NC State's Edibility field says: "Stems and leaves can be eaten, but when ingested in large quantities, can cause stomach upset." (not scoped to any animal). NC State's Problems field lists Contact Dermatitis and Weedy, and its tags include #contact dermatitis. RHS's Potentially harmful field says: "Sap can be a irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling". The NC State page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source names cats or dogs for Sedum acre (NC State has no Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags; RHS and MoBot give no animal-specific toxicity).

Weedy and aggressive note: NC State says moss stonecrop 'spreads aggressively' and 'It can be weedy and aggressive in some situations', and its Problems field lists Weedy; RHS says it 'may be invasive'. Spread should be contained and it can overwhelm other low plants.

is_edible is true only conditionally: NC State says stems and leaves can be eaten but large quantities can cause stomach upset; RHS does not address eating but flags irritant sap and NC State lists Contact Dermatitis; MoBot notes the epithet refers to an acrid taste. Treat as not a food plant for pets or children.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field also lists Partial Shade and its prose says 'site for sun to part sun', and MoBot says 'Good tolerance for light shade', but MoBot's Sun field and RHS's Position are Full sun only, so part_sun/part_shade were left out.

Korean Mint stands. On the RHS dedicated species page, the rendered heading block reads 'Agastache rugosa' / 'RHS Plant Profile' / 'Korean mint', so RHS leads with Korean mint, and 'wrinkled giant hyssop' sits under 'Other common names'. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetical (Blue Licorice, Indian Mint, Korean Mint, Patchouli Herb, Purple Giant Hyssop), so its first item is Blue Licorice. However, its Description opens with 'Korean Mint is found in the mountains regions of eastern Asia, especially along stream banks.', and that is verified verbatim. citations[0] cleanly supports the field. The other two common_name citations are <title> metadata (see citations[1] and citations[2]).

Provenance defect: '(Blue Licorice, Indian Mint, Korean Mint, Patchouli Herb, Purple Giant Hyssop)' is the page's <title> metadata. qc.py reports the <title> as 'Agastache rugosa (Blue Licorice, Indian Mint, Korean Mint, Patchouli Herb, Purple Giant Hyssop) | North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox', and the comma-joined string appears nowhere in the rendered body. The rendered Common Name(s) field stacks each name as a separate item, and Korean Mint is the third of five, not the lead. Any substitute would be a bare field value or a joined run of stacked items, which the rules forbid. Drop this citation, since citations[0] already carries common_name.

Provenance defect: 'Agastache rugosa | Korean mint' is the RHS page's <title> metadata. qc.py shows <title> = 'Agastache rugosa | Korean mint', and the pipe-joined string does not render on the page. The rendered page shows the binomial, 'RHS Plant Profile' and then 'Korean mint' as separate elements, so the only rendered substitute would be the bare name 'Korean mint', which is not allowed for a name claim. Drop it. The value stands on citations[0].

Agastache rugosa is correct and carries no author abbreviation. citations[3], 'Agastache rugosa is often confused with:', is rendered text on the NC State dedicated page and matches after whitespace normalisation. RHS's Name Status field reads 'Correct'. The RHS synonym 'Agastache foeniculum misapplied' points to a misapplication toward anise hyssop, not to a different accepted name for this taxon. No bleed from Agastache foeniculum was found in any value.

Same <title> metadata defect as citations[2]: 'Agastache rugosa | Korean mint' is the RHS <title> and is not rendered text. The rendered binomial is split across elements ('Agastache   rugosa'). The claim's parenthetical that the 'RHS Name Status field reads Correct' is accurate, but no rendered quote is offered for it, and 'Name Status Correct' would be a label+value concatenation. Drop it. scientific_name_accepted stands on citations[3].

['full_sun'] is well supported, and no bad entries need removing. NC State's structured Light field carries the single value 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', verified verbatim in citations[5]. RHS Position renders only 'Full sun'. NC State's description says 'Plant it in the full sun in well-draining soil.' Nothing supports part sun, and none was claimed.

Provenance defect: 'Position Full sun' joins the RHS label 'Position' to its separately rendered value 'Full sun'. The field value stands on citations[5]. If a second sun citation is wanted, use this verbatim NC State description sentence instead: 'Plant it in the full sun in well-draining soil.' Do not substitute the RHS Cultivation line 'Grow in reasonably well-drained soil in full sun with shelter': it may be genus-level boilerplate.

garden_bed is a valid single token, and citations[7] carries 'soil_base' in its claim label. The quote 'Mass plant or group it in the front of a border, in small spaces, walkways, or in cottage gardens.' is verbatim in NC State's Description.
